title: Comparison between architects and non-architects on perceptions of architectural acoustic environments
research_focus: To explore and compare the perceptions of architectural acoustic environments between architects and non-architects, develop theoretical frameworks for each group, analyze existing issues in acoustic environment design, and discuss potential solutions and development directions.

sample_context.description: 40 participants were interviewed, divided into an architect group (20 professionals with varying educational backgrounds and professional experiences) and a non-architect group (20 individuals with no background in architecture or acoustics, varying in age, educational backgrounds, and occupations). Participants were labeled AP01-AP20 for architects and NP01-NP20 for non-architects.
sample_context.setting: Online interviews conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic (January-May 2020).

findings.consequent: Positive attitude and willingness to invest
findings.source: 3.2. Attitudes towards the architectural acoustic environment
findings.theme_name: Non-architects' positive and supportive attitudes towards acoustic environment design
findings.description: Non-architects generally consider the acoustic environment an essential part of architectural space and are willing to pay for improvements, reflecting a positive and supportive attitude towards its design.
supporting_quotes: Architects should design a comfortable architectural acoustic environment, and so on. (NP18)
Of course, you cannot achieve the best of everything in building design. There will be some trade-offs, and it also depends on what is sacrificed for a beautiful sound. (NP11)

findings.source: 3.2. Attitudes towards the architectural acoustic environment
findings.theme_name: Architects' perception of difficulty and constraints in acoustic environment design
findings.description: Architects generally find it difficult to fully incorporate acoustic environment design into architectural design due to various constraints, including lack of client demand/budget, absence of clear design rules/cases, and insufficient software support.
supporting_quotes: It is difficult to grasp how to design the acoustic environment in the architectural space, and few of my colleagues pay attention to this matter. (AP10)
In general, our clients have little demand and budget for acoustic environment design. (AP2)

findings.consequent: Focus on physical parameters and noise control
findings.source: 3.3. Perceptions on the acoustic environment design
findings.theme_name: Architects' focus on physical parameters and noise control
findings.description: Architects primarily focus on controlling physical parameters like reverberation time, sound pressure level, and speech intelligibility, and consider acoustic design mainly for noise control, often after the architectural design is determined.
supporting_quotes: My idea is to use the partition and floor to ensure sound insulation. (AP11)
I think we must ensure speech intelligibility in the meeting room. (AP6)
Generally, architectural design is considered first, and acoustics design is considered after the architectural design has been determined. (AP1)

findings.consequent: Focus on elegant sounds and experiential quality
findings.source: 3.3. Perceptions on the acoustic environment design
findings.theme_name: Non-architects' focus on elegant sounds and experiential quality
findings.description: Non-architects prioritize the active use of elegant sounds, such as water sounds, to enhance their experience, making the environment feel pleasant, relaxed, and natural, rather than focusing on physical indicators.
supporting_quotes: We could create a pool inside the hall of the building. The water sound makes us feel natural and colourful. It could sooth my emotions during my daily work. (NP4)
I went to a restaurant which has a large waterscape. Various plants mingle with the water droplets and water sound. It is just like being among nature. (NP18)

findings.antecedent: Sound production method in acoustic environment design
findings.consequent: Preference for real sounds over audio systems
findings.source: 3.3. Perceptions on the acoustic environment design
findings.description: Both architects and non-architects generally prefer shaping real sounds within the environment, considering audio systems to be unnatural or 'too fake'.
supporting_quotes: We should try to create a real sound... If a loudspeaker is used to broadcast the voices, it would be too weird. (AP17)
Of course, it is good to shape the real sound. An audio system feels too fake. (NP9)

findings.antecedent: Factors influencing users' interpretation of acoustic environments
findings.consequent: Architects' insufficient attention to these factors
findings.theme_name: Architects' limited consideration of interpretation factors
findings.description: Architects primarily focus on group characteristics (e.g., building function) when considering user interpretation, struggling to incorporate individual factors like personal preferences, emotional states, and physical conditions into their designs.
supporting_quotes: Each user has different feelings, but the architectural space usually serves multiple people. It's contradictory to cater to all tastes. (AP1)
Some users stay for a long time, some for a short time, some are sad, and some are happy. We can't take all these into account in the architectural design. (AP6)

findings.consequent: Interpretation influenced by expectation, personal state, and preference
findings.description: Non-architects' interpretation of acoustic environments is significantly influenced by their expectations (based on building function and prior experience), personal states (sensitivity, fatigue, emotions), and individual preferences (activity type, judgment of quietness).
supporting_quotes: My wife is in poor health, so I often go to the hospital. The hospital has been noisy for many years, and I am used to it. (NP15)
I think I can only pay attention to the acoustic environment when I have energy. If I'm very tired from work on any given day, I don't care about these things at all. (NP8)
Sometimes, feelings depend on one's mood. (NP9)

findings.consequent: Perception of outcome limited to user-architectural space interaction
findings.theme_name: Architects' limited perception of acoustic environment outcomes
findings.description: Architects' perception of the outcomes of acoustic environments is primarily focused on user interaction with architectural space (e.g., yearning, escape, adaptation), often neglecting the profound, long-term impacts on users' behavior, emotion, recovery, and health.
supporting_quotes: In ancient Chinese buildings, there is a design method that allows the user to hear an attractive sound before seeing the building; the area can be invisible in advance. (AP2)

Some noise is unavoidable, and office workers, including myself, have adapted to the sound of the keyboard and printer. I sometimes wear headphones to isolate myself from the acoustic environment. (AP5)

findings.consequent: Influence on behaviour, emotion, recovery, and health
findings.theme_name: Non-architects' broad perception of acoustic environment outcomes
findings.description: Non-architects perceive the acoustic environment as having profound and long-term impacts on their behavior, emotions, recovery from stress, and overall health, with outcomes varying based on individual preferences.
supporting_quotes: When I'm at work, I like to stay in a quiet place during lunchtime and refresh myself. (NP5)
My workplace is close to the corridor, and people walk around and make phone calls all day, which makes me very irritable. (NP9)

Architects design a good public space with a graceful acoustic environment for us in the community, so everyone enjoys playing and exercising there; we will then make friends and improve our mood and health. (NP10)

findings.antecedent: Architects' understanding of active architectural acoustic environment design
findings.consequent: Insufficient ability to overcome inherent limitations
findings.source: 4.1. Issues on the design of the acoustic environment
findings.theme_name: Architects' insufficient understanding of active acoustic design
findings.description: Architects' grasp of active architectural acoustic environment design is not sufficient to overcome its inherent limitations, leading to a relatively passive state in considering and implementing acoustic design.

findings.antecedent: Architects' understanding of public preferences and demands for acoustic environments
findings.consequent: Lack of clear objectives and motivation for acoustic design
findings.source: 4.1. Issues on the design of the acoustic environment
findings.theme_name: Architects' insufficient understanding of public needs
findings.description: Architects lack a sufficient understanding of public preferences and demands regarding acoustic environments, which results in a lack of clear objectives and motivation for engaging in intense acoustic environment design.

derived_hypotheses: Integrating acoustic design holistically into the overall architectural design process, rather than as a separate consideration, will lead to more effective and user-satisfying acoustic environments.
Providing architects with design language-based rules, software support, and adequate budget for acoustic environment design will improve their ability to create positive acoustic environments.

Establishing effective and routine communication and feedback mechanisms (e.g., post-occupancy evaluations with 'rewards' for acoustic design) will increase architects' motivation and understanding of public preferences and demands.

Shifting architects' design thinking from solely noise control to proactively considering the behavioral, emotional, recovery, and health outcomes for users will lead to the creation of more supportive and multi-level acoustic environments.
Designing for 'resonance' and consistency between the acoustic environment and architectural space, rather than over-emphasizing uniqueness, will provide users with better immersive experiences.
mechanism_candidates: A holistic design approach allows for the consideration of multiple interacting factors (scale, material, function, emotion, context) from the outset, preventing conflicts and enabling a balanced audio-visual experience (MSI, EC, PP).
Design rules and tools reduce perceived difficulty and provide concrete guidance, lowering cognitive load and increasing controllability for architects (PP, DP, A9_Task_Cognition).
Feedback mechanisms provide architects with data on user preferences and outcomes, reducing prediction error and reinforcing design choices that align with user satisfaction (PP, NM - reward).

A broader focus on human well-being outcomes encourages architects to design for a multi-level acoustic environment that caters to diverse user needs and promotes restorative experiences (DT, NM, IC, ART, SRT).
Sensory congruence and consistency between acoustic and architectural elements reduce cognitive load and prediction error, fostering a sense of immersion and comfort (MSI, PP).
transferability_limits: The study's findings are based on interviews with Chinese architects and non-architects, and perceptions may differ in other regions and cultures due to variations in design concepts and concerns.
limitations: All interviewees were Chinese architects, and design concepts and concerns may differ in other regions and cultures.
The study was conducted online due to the COVID-19 pandemic, which might have influenced the interaction dynamics.
